title: Whittled sycamore salt scoop
subtitle: Seasoned sycamore: a small scoop for salt, spices, and loose tea
excerpt: A small hand-whittled scoop for salt, loose tea, or ground spice. Sycamore dries food-safe and pale, carves cleanly with a sloyd knife in seasoned state, and resists moisture absorption better than most food-safe timbers. The whole scoop is cut from a small offcut, no axe needed.
sourceNotes: Cassell's Cyclopaedia of Mechanics vol. III (1885) for the treen scoop form; Newey & Drage Practical Carpentry for seasoned sycamore in food-use items.

glossaryTerms.definition: A short straight-bladed knife with a stout handle; the Swedish school-craft standard for whittling and carving.
The rough-shaped piece of wood from which the finished item is carved.

content.text: A sycamore salt scoop is a small, narrow-bowled scoop roughly 10 cm long, the right size for a salt cellar or a spice jar. Sycamore is the traditional dairy and food-use timber in Britain: pale, food-safe, and resistant to moisture uptake between washes. The scoop uses a single small offcut of seasoned sycamore with no specialist tools beyond a sloyd knife and a small hook knife.
Grip: four-finger grip on the work; thumb-push grip on the knife. Never make a cut whose blade-path can reach a body part.
Cut direction: push cuts (blade away from body) and thumb-pivot cuts are the default. Pull cuts only with the work braced against the chest and the blade-arc unable to reach anything vital.
Sharpening: a dull tool is more dangerous than a sharp one, the dull tool slips. Strop every fifteen minutes of carving, hone weekly, oilstone monthly.
First aid: keep a styptic pencil, gauze, and a clean dressing within reach. Apply firm pressure, elevate, and dress. A cut that shows fat or won't close with pressure goes to A&E, not a plaster.
Workspace: stable seat, good light, no children or pets within arm-and-blade reach.

One piece of seasoned sycamore, 12 cm long, 3 cm wide, 1.5 cm thick, grain running along the length. A woodworking offcut or a short length of dowel-section sycamore works. Birch or maple are direct substitutes, same food-safe pale timber. Moisture content 8, 12% for indoor use.
A carving stool or a low chair. Good light. The scoop is small enough to be done entirely in the lap with a leather apron.

Step 2: Shape the back and handle
Turn the blank over. Use push cuts to carve the back of the bowl into a shallow dome, 4 mm depth at the centre. Taper the handle from 10 mm at the shoulder to 7 mm at the end. Use
for the final shaping around the bowl shoulder.

Use the hook knife, small, to hollow the bowl to about 5 mm depth at the centre. Work in arcs from the far rim toward yourself. Keep the wall even, 2, 3 mm is sufficient for a salt scoop, which carries no mechanical load.
Apply raw linseed oil. Soak for one hour, wipe off the surplus, repeat after twenty-four hours. Cure for two weeks before food contact.
Tea scoop: same shape, 6 cm handle, slightly narrower bowl for a caddy or small tin.
Sugar spoon: slightly wider and shallower bowl, longer handle for a sugar bowl.
Wipe clean with a dry cloth between uses. Hand wash occasionally and dry immediately. Re-oil when the wood looks dry.

attrs.symptom: The bowl surface is ridged from hook-knife passes
attrs.cause: Passes not overlapping enough or blade blunt
attrs.fix: Strop the hook knife and overlap each arc by at least half the blade width. A finishing pass with the knife held at a very shallow angle, almost scraping, evens the surface.
